Zay Flowers draws a plus matchup — IND concede 68 yds/game to WR1s (league ~58), and BAL funnel 26% of targets his way. A rec-yards spot.

The IND welcome the BAL as underdogs of 3.5, with the total set at 49.5 — a market that implies a BAL 26–23 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 33% of its snaps with BAL in front, 42% within one score, and 25% with BAL chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

A modest edge to BAL. They should lead more often than not, tilting them slightly toward the run late, while IND leans a touch more pass-heavy to stay in it — but the effect is gentle; this isn't a script that dramatically reshapes anyone's usage.

The Key Matchups

Tough sledding for Jonathan Taylor — BAL are stingy against the run (94 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

Lamar Jackson has a passing-yards tailwind — IND allow 253 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Daniel Jones has a passing-yards tailwind — BAL allow 257 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Mark Andrews has room to work — IND allow 42 yds/game to TE1s (vs ~35), a receiving-yards and target angle.

Alec Pierce draws a plus matchup — BAL concede 74 yds/game to WR1s (league ~58). A rec-yards spot.

Touchdown Board

Derrick Henry is a bell-cow (76% of carries) meeting a defense that allows 0.47 RB rushing TDs/game — strong anytime-TD equity.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

A modest lean to BAL — they should lead more often than not, nudging them toward the run late and giving Derrick Henry a gentle game-script tailwind.

BAL — a run-heavy offense

BAL are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 30% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

This is the profile that most rewards a lead back. As a 4-point favorite projected to lead for 33% of snaps, BAL will be running to close the game, and their run-first identity compounds it. Derrick Henry is the beneficiary — we project 16 carries for 76 yards, and his ceiling is where the value sits: in the simulations where this becomes a two-score game, his volume spikes as BAL salt it away.

The flip side: Zay Flowers (6 targets, 57 yards) has his ceiling capped by the same script that helps the run game — when BAL lead and run, there simply aren't as many pass attempts to go around. He's a safer floor than ceiling play in this spot.

Underneath, Mark Andrews (TE, 3 targets, 29 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

IND — a balanced offense

IND are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (44% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Game script works against the run here — IND project to trail and throw, which squeezes Jonathan Taylor's rushing projection (16 carries, 76 yards) but raises his value as a receiver; trailing teams check the ball down, and his target share ticks up as the game gets away from them.

Alec Pierce is the one to target from a volume standpoint: as underdogs throwing to keep pace, IND funnel work to their top receiver — 5 targets for 50 yards projected, with genuine upside if they fall behind early and the game turns one-dimensional.

Underneath, Tyler Warren (TE, 6 targets, 46 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 4-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
